review: I used to be able to say "yes, get this game," but now that you've taken it's predecessor offline, I cannot and won't. How long do we have, maybe another 2 to 3 years for this game? Possibly even less because of your focus on the other game? I don't like modern Forza games, but at least they let you play their older games even without an online connection. If you can't even do that for your consumers, then why bother make anymore games?

This game was once a haven, once a miracle. It was an actually good racing game in the modern era. A rarity. But then The Chase happened. Before The Chase released in November 2020, I played this game almost every single day. I no-lifed it, grinded out every event, car, part, you name it. It was my favorite game. Then The Chase came along and ruined everything. It removed the ways to get the secondary currency (Crew Credits) by doing Daily tasks. Instead, the only way to get this currency now? Pay REAL MONEY. They also added the "Motorpass" system which locks a ton of content behind a paywall. These mechanics are horrific and make the game feel like a F2P, but it's a paid game! Absolutely ridiculous. I, along with many players, stopped playing after The Chase released and permanently changed the game for the worse. I finally came back to it a few days ago just for the game to almost explode my GPU because the PC port of this game is absolutely atrocious for optimization and decided "enough is enough. It's time to let go." I will be uninstalling the game after posting this review, but before I do let me run down every reason why you should not play this game, or at least be very weary about doing so.

-Optimization. I have a very decent rig, and yet this game THROTTLES my computer. Not to mention the game constantly crashes, and sometimes will lock up your computer for upwards of 20 minutes by doing so. If you still want to play this game after reading this, PLEASE consider playing a console port instead. As I said, this game could very well cause damage to your computer if you don't take caution. The game almost caused my GPU to break before I uninstalled it.

-Monetization. As I said in the first part of this review, The Chase introduced very predatory microtransactions into the the game. They are not forced, but they lock a lot of content behind a paywall and try to bait you into buying it. Very scummy.

-Repetition/Bland single player experience. The single player experience gets very repetitive and boring. The game has a very obvious bias to Street Racer events. There are 50 different Street Race events in the game. For perspective, no other class in the game breaks 20 unique events. Most classes don't break *10*. The game advertises itself as having tons of different vehicles and event types, but really it only focuses on Street Race. This applies to updates too, as 90% of the new events and cars that get added are Street Race or Hypercar class. On top of all of this, the singleplayer ai is ridiculously easy. The "Races" are more or less time trials with ai. Do not expect a challenging and enthralling singleplayer experience.

-Lack of understanding between devs and players. The devs do NOT listen to the feedback of the players, they just do as they please. The community went up in flames after The Chase, but the devs issued one statement that boiled down to "we don't care, keep whining". They do not listen. They do not care. The playerbase means nothing to them besides a means to make money. Do not expect the devs to do the right thing.

-Lack of variety. For a game that advertises itself for being diverse and varied, it sure isn't. The basegame gave us some variety sure, but all the content updates add the most generic and boring cars possible. Not to mention that other vehicle types such as boats, planes, bikes, etc NEVER get new content. They might add a new bike once every few months, but you will never see new boats or planes or other vehicles. And yet they will add pointless reskins of existing cars that nobody asked for all day long... They very obviously only care about adding the most predictable and uninteresting vehicles possible, so don't let the promise of variety fool you. You could easily get a similar car list out of other franchises.

-Boring events. This goes back to the boring and repetitive nature of the game, but most of the events are very boring and uninteresting layouts. There's a few good ones, but most of the tracks are extremely simple and easy. Very few sharp turns or hairpins, no traffic in races, overly long and tedious, etc. The ai will not pose a threat, and the track layouts will bore you to death after you play for a while.

-Empty and bland map. Lots of copy/paste in the map, lots of stretches of empty road, lots of areas lacking detail and feeling soullessly void of life, lots of extremely condensed towns and cities, it just feels like a very cheap map and is actually a downgrade from The Crew's map. No joke, look it up on YouTube. They downgraded the map bewteen games and it shows. A lot.

I had positive things to say about this game some months back, but all of my good will and love for the game has evaporated. I will still list some of the good things this game does however, just to be fair.

-Livery Editor. It has a good livery editor. I made plenty of detailed skins in my time playing the game. It's not the best, but it's pretty good. You can easily make good stuff with it and it's fairly limitless.

-Decent physics. They aren't phenominal and they certainly have their bad moments, but overall the physics are pretty light and fun. Rallycross cars especially are fun to just take on some dirt roads and rip it up with.

-Playability. You can't blow through the entire game in a few days, it does keep you coming back to play more. Money rewards are fairly low to make you work for what you want. The issue being that it takes that to an extreme and ends up becoming a bit tedious and boring. It has enough to keep you coming back, but maybe a bit too much.

Would I reccomend this game? No. Not anymore. I would and have reccomended the game to many people and friends since it came out in 2018, but after the last few months of the game's life I cannot support it anymore. Things started falling off in Summer 2020, but The Chase in Nov 2020 sealed it's fate. No longer can I enjoy this game, or advise others to play it. If you *still* want to play it, please do not play the PC version. You will regret it. Buy a console port, like PS4 or Xbox. They are far more stable (but still have issues. I played on PS4 and still had the game crash). I would seriously advise you to save your money, or maybe watch the updates for a few months in hopes that the studio gets their act together and brings the game back to it's glory days of 2019. I hope this review helps at least one person understand that this game is not what it once was, and that their money is better spent elsewhere.

TLDR: The game used to be really good but from Summer 2020 until now it has gotten progressively worse to the point where it's no longer worth playing. Buy something else or wait a few months to see if they fix the game with update, but  don't hold your breath.

PREFACE:
If you're wondering why I already have this many hours even though the game just launched hours ago, it is because I purchased the Ultimate Edition, and was able to play 3 days early via Early Access. Also, I put in over 200 hours into the first game of the series on Xbox One, and put in about 20+ hours into Beta for this game. I skipped through everything I was able to do in the Beta, and grinded my way up to Icon, so that I felt I had enough experience to make this review.

GAMEPLAY:
This is where this game shines. I thoroughly enjoy the driving in this game. I came into it expecting to hate the boats/airplanes, and thought about ignoring them altogether, but instead I fell in love with them. I refuse to fast travel (except for the parts that I completed in the Beta), but now I find myself boating and/or flying to almost every race. The most important mechanic is the driving, and that feels great. Every vehicle in the game appears to drive differently, and have a unique weight that gives a great feeling to driving. 

One of the biggest complaints of the Beta was how you could grind the rails and not lose any speed whatsoever, but Ubi
has seemed to fix that at this point. Being in a vehicle is fun in this game, and that is important, considering that this is a racing game. Rubberbanding is a huge issue though, and detracts from the races themselves. The first title thrived on cross-country races, but what's the point of a 40 minute race, if only the last minute is all that matters? This needs to be sorted out. It almost encourages you to sit behind first place and conserve your nitrous until the last second.

The thing that can make gameplay SO aggravating is the GPS. They completely removed the arrows that you used to be able to follow on top of the screen. Now all you get is the tiny GPS off to the bottom right corner of the screen, and sometimes it can be impossible to follow, especially at extremely fast speeds. Unfortunately, that is not the only problem with the GPS. Half the time it doesn't even work, and just gives you a straight line to the location, and you have no idea how to get where you are going, so opt to fly there.

STORY/CHARACTERS:
There is no story. A lot of people thought the story from the first game was quite boring, but was this really the solution for that? The characters serve no purpose, and bring no attachment to who they are. Right now this game is a single-player grind fest. Also, I don't know who did the animations for the characters in the game, but it looks like they hired the BioWare B-Team that did Mass Effect Andromeda. It's bad.

MULTIPLAYER:
It is nonexistent. You can hook up with friends and drive around, but that is the ONLY form of multiplayer in the game, besides leaderboards for races. The fact that this game launched without PvP is an insult to the consumer. How can a game possibly be sold as an MMO-lite racer with no PvP? Right now the grind is for nothing, and we have no solid launch date for PvP. If you are looking to do online races, then do not purchase this game yet.

VISUALS:
This game is beautiful. But only certain aspects. They nailed the two most important parts of racers, and that is the cars and lighting. The cars look absolutely stunning, and is a huge leap in the right direction for the series, even more than the last game's Wild Run expansion. Ironically, I also noted lighting as looking good. And that's true.....partially. The god rays in this game are among the best I've seen in a vanilla game. The lighting of the sky always captures the mood, and is generally quite gorgeous. Where does the lighting fail? In the headlights. It is IMPOSSIBLE to see in the dark, unless you are in a lit city. The distance of your headlights is a problem the community has raised since the Alpha state, but nothing appears to have been fixed in that area.

The landscapes are quite pretty, but what ruins it are the popins. Yes I have a GTX 1060, but look at any review. This is a problem across all platforms, even for people with 1080 TIs. Ubi has addressed this, saying that it had something to do with the draw distance forced by allowing planes in the game, but in truth, this does nothing but prove that Ubi is acknowledging that their game is not fully optimized, even though it is now launch day. I think it's pretty unacceptable to have a 1080 TI not be able to handle the popins, even when at 1080p.

The water is gorgeous, and is one of the saving graces for the environment. One of the reasons I travel by boat so much in this game is because the water is pretty, unique, fun, and doesn't have all the foliage popins. 

The worst part about the graphics in this game are the buildings. They look like Legos, like something out of a game that came in the previous decade. It's so weird having a game that looks so beautiful in some aspects, but absolutely abysmal in others.

AUDIO:
The audio in this game has caused a bunch problems for me. The amount of bugs is crazy. Half the time you will hear a car coming up right behind you, only to look behind you and see no one. Also if you crash into objects in the world, there is a bug that repeats the crashing sound on end until you pause the game. 

The voice acting is pretty unfortunate. A lot of voices didn't match their faces/animations, and it sounds like Ubi just picked up random people off the street, used a subpar mic, and gave them really bad and cheezy lines to say.

The cars do sound nice, and especially the backfiring of cars can be really satisfying.

The music within the game's radiostations are also much more satisfying than the original game's.

ECONOMY:
This game's economy has been VERY inconsistent from the start. Many cars didn't match each other in terms of price, and although they have addressed this slightly, the problem still rings true.

So, is the game P2W? Yeah. It definitely is. Right now, you can purchase a 2nd form of currency, and buy any car you want. I'm not saying microtransactions are the worst thing in the world, but when they are taken further than just cosmetics, I tend to have a problem with it. Right now you can spend extra cash, and compete on the leaderboards with any car in the game from the get-go. Imagine if PvP was actually in this game? Ubi is practically encouraging players to spend money to get everything from the start, and discouraging them from actually even playing the game at all.

VALUE:
I'd say it would take the average player about 20 hours to get Icon, and unlock mostly everything in the game. You can get more time of course by grinding out the Icon ranks and such, but I would only see players doing this in prepping for PvP. By using the Dollar per Hour scale, that costs the average consumer about $3 per hour. That's not terrible value, but if this game launched without missing content, you would get much more value per dollar. At least most won't get the Ultimate edition like I did and decrease the value even more.

FINAL THOUGHTS:
The Crew launched as a an absolute mess. I don't think that anyone will say otherwise, even Ubisoft. It showed by how much effort they put into resurrecting that game from the dead. They updated the graphics, and also put out two of the best expansions in recent video game history besides the Witcher 3. To me, The Crew launched at about a 4/10. That's how much of a mess that game was. After Ubisoft fixed it, they got it to about an 8.5 in my books. I picked it up for free on Games with Gold, and it quickly became my favorite racing game after all of the expansions. And yes, this is coming from a Forza fanboy. The Crew had a slow start, but eventually gave itself a solid foundation for a sequel. Unfortunately what we got was a game with much better mechanics, yet stripped of all of it's basic content. It is with a heavy heart that I have to give such a bad review of my most anticipated game of the year, that's not named Smash Bros. Ultimate.

VERDICT:
6.5/10

Alright. [i]The Crew 2[/i]. Judging from the current all-time high concurrent peak player counts for the game, I'd say a lot of people are aware of this game currently being priced at one dollar (and less in some regions). And a lot of people have bought the game as a result of this stunning deal. Including myself. Just to get it out of the way, if you have something to say about The Crew 1's removal, go to the game forum. I'm not interested in the topic as part of this review. So...

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3329984820

I am confident I would never have bought this game had it not been a buck, and I'm also confident that a lot of people have the same opinion. But since it was a buck, I did in fact buy it, and I'm glad I did. It's hella fun. The gameplay loop of joining events and races, using the cash you earn to buy new vehicles and such, and upgrading your vehicles with loot rewards from events and races, is pretty simple. But it is also effective. As you progress, you will unlock more events and races, and because they are located across the lower 48 States, you get a wide variety of settings for everything. From cities to mountains to forests to lakes to deserts to meteor craters to rain to snow to beaches and on and on, there is a vast array of different types of courses and tracks to enjoy. And there are a wide variety of types of races and events as well. From standard track races to boat races to plane aerobatics to demolition derbies, and so on.

The sheer volume of content is quite impressive. And, the various vehicles, be they cars or trucks or bikes or planes or boats or dune buggies or whatever...they all handle nicely and feel good to drive in. Each of these is upgradeable in many ways, which will increase their performance, handling, speed, and just generally make them function better and better as you progress.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3329984770

There is a campaign of sorts, where you try to become the lead racer in a few different styles, but it's also easy enough to ignore that in favor of simply racing around, upgrading your vehicles, wandering around your crib, and simply free roaming. And free roaming is a lot of fun in and of itself. Mostly, it's a huge sightseeing trip, where you can also try to beat other player's records with jumps, speed, and so on; that you come across while driving around. And setting some records of your own for other people to beat. And there is a decent photography mini game all across the States where you will take pictures of animals, special vehicles and such to gain more cash and follower.

And gaining followers is really the sub goal that most impacts your playthrough. The number of followers you have determines how popular your racer is, which in turn unlocks new vehicle options and race/event options. Just about everything you do will earn you new followers (and cash).

Also, you can play with other players and even if you're not, you will see them all over the map. At this moment in time (the time of this review being written), no matter where you are, somebody else is nearby. And there are a lot of player created activities as well. Plus, you can co-op with friends if you get bored of solo play. So really, the content just keeps expanding as you explore what the game has to offer.

Visually, the game looks great. It has a 60 FPS cap, which isn't anything to brag about, but somehow, the devs have made the most out of that limitation and made a game that has a never-ending supply of screenshot moments. The audio is also well done. The songs themselves are very cool. The dialogue is basically all "hey bro" Extreme Games fodder, but it's fun and definitely appropriate.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3330111663

You will need Ubisoft Connect to play this. I don't care at all about that, but you might. And some people are having an issue with the game crashing if they have other non-Steam clients linked to their Ubi account. I have not had that issue personally and have it linked to both PSN and Epic as well, but if you do, you will need to unlink everything except Steam and that will resolve the crashing issue apparently. No idea how or why that is what it is or why it only affects some players. It's been a bug free experience for me though with a 3070 and an i5.

Now, should you also buy the season pass? I personally have no intention of doing so. There's no new content, and I don't care about getting a few extra cars and some swag. But the base game, offering what can easily be hundreds and even thousands of hours of content for one dollar. That is something I can definitely get behind. I can't think of a better deal in gaming at this moment. Now, if you miss or skip this one-dollar promotion they have going on right now, value will be more of...you know..., a [i]your mileage may vary[/i] type thing....

If I had to sum up this game in one word, that word would be "inconsistent". The core racing experience is fun, and the open-world is still a thrill to just fly, race and drift around. However, there are definetly some irks that hold it back:

"That's solid? really?" - you'll find yourself saying this a fair bit, unfortunately. Whilst bus shelters, mailboxes, lampposts and even traffic fold up like they're made of crisps and ping off into space, trees and parked cars are merciless, utterly solid, and occasionally placed exactly where you think you can get that little shortcut.

The AI: Rubberband doesnt even sum the AI up. In fact, it's barely worth trying to drive fast, as they will ALWAYS catch up to you and press their hidden hyperspace buttons the second you overcook a corner. Incredabily frustrating sometimes when you've been in the lead for 95% of the race, then get taken out by a suprise bus on the last corner and finish stone-dead last. Hard mode races up the challenge significantly, but dont be surprised to see the AI disappear over the draw distance within 10 seconds of the start if you havn't grinded out those upgrades for your vehicles.

The Story: If I had to guess, I'd say The Crew 2 was designed to be faaaar more ambitious in it's storytelling. The cutscenes and dialogue you get occasionally before or after a race feel really disjointed, as if there's a big chunk of the story you missed somewhere. One place it particularly confised me was one of the Rival races, where suddenly the mentor who's been urging you on all this time suddenly heel turns so rapidly it's surprising he doesnt do himself an injury, and opens a cutscene by telling your mechanic, Hiro, that you've somehow betrayed him and he wants a race... by doing what he wanted you to and winning races... huh? It just made me confused. Add to this the artsy cutscenes full of pseudo-philosophical commentary that honestly makes zero sense to pop up when they do, and overall the impression that there was a lot of story removed that might have linked these sections together can't be ignored.

There is a lot of good though. The racing is fun, the sensation of speed is excellent, the environments (especially out in the countryside with deserts and the Grand Canyon) are gorgeous and run well, and it really shines when you're just having fun in the open world. Just not in Monster Trucks. Never Monster Trucks. They just... no. horrible.

To sum up, there is a huge amount of potential here. It just needs filling out, and as such in it's present state I can't really recommend it for full price. Maybe after a few updates, it will start to fulfil it's potential. So who made this game again? Oh. Ubisoft. Don't count on the potential being filled then.

PSA: I'm honestly super surprised I actually have to explain this here but to everyone commenting about the problem being connection or cpu or w/e else, rubberbanding ai is not a term for lagging. Rubber band AI refers to a feature of artificial intelligence found in racing titles that is designed to prevent players from getting too far ahead of computer-controlled opponents.

Neutrals:
- There are 25-minute single races. In an arcade racing game. I hated this. You may not.

Pros:
- Most of the time, it ran at 60 FPS.
- Large map, but...

Cons:
- There is little to see on the map that's interesting. Sometimes the trees change type, and maybe there's more water in an area.
- The upgrade system is painfully bad and is essentially a lootbox minus a box. You win a race, you get some random upgrades. You can have, say, LVL 65 in every part but one and it may take you 20 races to get an upgrade for that slot. Yes, you can get RNG'd into having to grind races to upgrade. It's as bad as it sounds.
- VERY hard to read tracks when racing. Sometimes you'll just go in the wrong direction because you have no clue where you are intended to go. You essentially have to watch the minimap because watching the race itself is useless as the tracks are signposted more poorly than any other racing game I've played in recent memory.
- The AI is tuned incredibly poorly. Either they're WAY ahead of you even though you're driving a better car and the race is half your level, or you're absolutely demolishing them. There is no adjusting this. It is infuriating.
- All the cars control like they're racing on butter. Everything slides uncontrollably and really shows off how shoddy the physics are in this game. You will constantly careen into stuff. And speaking of...
- Hitting damn near anything brings you to a complete stop. You don't slide past stuff like other arcade racing games when the corner of your car clips a bush, you come to a complete halt. You now have to restart the race because you WILL NOT catch up. Is the race 12 minutes long? Too bad. Now to find that race reset...
- The menus are awful. I had to actually Google how to restart a race and quit the game. Thought they'd be in the in-game menus? Hah, you simpleton! You have to hit Y to bring up a special menu that hides in the corner of the screen, but only comes up while driving! Want that menu on a keyboard & mouse? NOPE! Those buttons sometimes show up at the bottom of a different menu where you may have expected them in the first place! Well, sometimes. Only when the option for the buttons feels like appearing. Sometimes it just doesn't.
- The characters are astoundingly annoying and are written to speak like a Red Bull commercial. The overtly positive "might as well be saying nothing at all" style garbage non-speaking flows out of everyone's mouth continually. The story is non-existant. If you love chasing "followers" (ugh), then go on Instagram and be vapid there. Even the shell of a life you pretend to have there will be more fun than The Crew 2.
- Very odd and frequent framerate drops when physics items interact with each other. This happens often. Adjusting settings did not help.
- It looks worse than the original did somehow, and the first was quite an ugly game.
- One of the worst game soundtracks I've heard since Gone Home. This low-budget mess of a soundtrack complete with incredibly shrill lady-punk songs. The only good song on the soundtrack is Airbourne - Running Wild, and it's over 10 years old. Yes that's an opinion, and your mileage may vary.
- I am an idiot and preordered the Gold Edition because, hey, this is a sequel. It's going to improve on the original in many ways. (Narrator: "It did not.") They didn't listen to a single damn complaint about the original, even though nearly every review both professional and amateur said the same things (Many of which are pointed out in my review here). This makes me madder. You couldn't even be bothered to fix the obvious? Bad form, Ubisoft.
- They haven't improved on any of these complaints since launch and instead insist on putting out boring Live Events. This is because Live games make more money (See Destiny). Make no mistake, this is a product, not art and it definitely wants all of your money.
- I genuinely tried to like it and power through some of the issues, but I just can't any more. I hate this game. It is one of the worst racing games I have played in recent memory. Even the two most recent Need For Speed games were better, and they were mediocre at the best of times.

As I played about 200+ hours in The Crew 1 I have to admit that in The Crew 2 I got bored after 20 hours already.

1. Price - way too much for this game. Wait for a sale if you REALLY want to play it BADLY. I didn't have fun when playing this game, which shocked me though, because The Crew 1 brought me so much fun. Very disappointing. 
2. Map - landmarks are gone, they kinda replaced it with Photo Albums, which is not that bad, however it's kinda annoying (at least for me). 4. Vehicles - probably the biggest plus in this game. There's a wide range of cars, etc., however, with all the classes (boats, planes) it doesn't feel like a REAL racing game anymore.

All nice places, which I enjoyed in The Crew 1 just for the nature are now covered with stupid banners and fancy lights, etc. etc. which takes the feeling away. The whole "story" is just a collection of short events, which are apparently huge in the so called TV.

[b]What it is:[/b]
A massive open-world driving game that boasts the greatest map ever made in its genre but is screaming for more polish in virtually every aspect.

[b]What it does well:[/b]
[list]
[*]That map - a 1:40 scale recreation of the United States lifted from the original game but updated to accommodate essentially every type of motorized mobility with unparalleled variety
[*]A genuinely liberating sense of freedom from a game structured to reward you for doing virtually anything in any vehicle anywhere (except for the PvP)
[*]The [i]second[/i]-best game on the planet for relaxation behind Microsoft Flight Simulator - The Crew 2 is at its best not when you're racing but when you're treating it as a giant high-speed walking simulator with no story to speak of
[*]An amusingly varied vehicle list that goes from the usual genre staples to things like a biplane, a helicopter, a hovercraft, and more
[*]An equally varied array of activity types to engage in - including drift and drag races, aerial stunt challenges, monster truck arenas, demolition derbies, and more
[*]A great photo mode held back only by the game's own visual inconsistencies
[*]The weekly summits provide a fairly compelling reason to regularly revisit the game to do more than just cruise and chill out
[*]Free updates for 29 months and counting
[/list]

[b]What it fluffs:[/b]
[list]
[*]Despite already having hundreds of races in the game, the map still feels underused with loads of unused open spaces and roads
[*]No open-world PvP races - a feature that existed in 2007's Test Drive Unlimited
[*]No open-world or multiplayer police chases
[*]A loot system that seems to be entertaining and somewhat addictive at first, but eventually proves to be generally pointless outside of some top-tier gear sets
[*]The environments feel really dated now the second you stop to look, and both draw distance and LOD handling could use an improvement
[*]As of late 2020, nights are [i]still[/i] "broken" by design and way too bright due to the developers' inability to properly implement car headlights
[*]Strange vehicle physics engine that still doesn't know how to handle collisions convincingly
[*]A cheating AI that relies only on stupid levels of rubberbanding to stay competitive
[*]Strange UI/UX decisions - chief among them the refusal to save your location upon quitting the game and always forcing you to start each session either at home or an HQ
[*]This game has an exceptional number of vehicle types for you to enjoy, but the number of vehicles available in each type is actually pretty underwhelming
[*]Horrible story and writing with the only saving grace being how easily they can all be ignored
[*]The updates may be free, but content is delivered as a painfully slow drip feed and a lot of the "new" cars are just reskins of the old ones
[*]Paywalled seasonal content that doesn't seem to offer any real value
[/list]

[b]Technical stuff:[/b]
[list]
[*]Disappointingly capped at 60fps like its predecessor, but it stays locked at 60fps quite easily too
[*]Tons of environmental graphical assets that look like they're from 15 years ago if you stop to look and yet still pass for good looking when you're rolling by at 320km/h
[*]Almost complete ultrawide support - HUD and UI are not stretched but remain confined to 16:9 screen space
[*]Occasional minor connectivity issues
[*]For some reason may become unstable when played with a Bluetooth controller
[*]If you have two controllers connected to your PC (e.g. Xbox pad and flight stick), remove one before you start playing because this game idiotically takes input from all devices simultaneously
[/list]

[b]Recommendation:[/b]
The Crew 2 does do the basics right, but none of those basics can compete with what's on offer in Forza Horizon titles. You're basically here for the map or nothing else, and even that amazing map remains underutilized. The graphics engine appears in need of an overhaul as some serious issues involving pop-in and brightness at night remain unsolved almost two years after launch. It's a good buy for those who loved the first Crew - and its spiritual predecessors, the two Test Drive Unlimited games - and no one else.

[i] My impression of the game kept on changing at each progressing 5 hours interval. This review was framed after investing 30+ hours into the game and concluding the final rivalry races. The initial hours were so repulsive and full of meh impressions. But once you get a hold of a particular vehicle type and its handling, it’s all fun and excitement.[/i]

[h1][b] 📝Story/Plot:[/b][/h1]
Just a generic plot setup to give your grind some motive and goal. A rookie entering the world of racing and guess what, some organizers see his potential and gave him a chance without even seeing him race beforehand. Just be #1 all around the events and conclude your journey after beating the top dogs who were the organizers too.

[h1][b]🎮Gameplay:[/b][/h1]
[b]Initial impression-[/b]
Imagine a hot girl with no personality. That’s the first 5-minute impression of The Crew 2. Starting off with high budget cinematics and performing short lap segment races while shifting to a new vehicle again and again. Sounds cool right? Wait until you see the whole f*cking world curve like in the movie Inception and Doctor Strange. At this point, my jaw was indisputably touching the ground. But just after completing a normal event race, it hit me with gloom and awkwardness. All that cinematic brag of “Speed is Life” and bla bla comes down to a slow race with the road looking like a low texture road. Like WTF?

[b]Mechanics/Controllability-[/b]
I know it’s not a real sim racing game, nor advertised as a pure arcade. It’s unique on its own. But I feel like not giving it a category works as a bypass for some faulty mechanics. Cars feel slightly slow and weigh a ton on the controller. The purpose of a racing game is to acknowledge the speed atmosphere, which was only endured with top cars. Cars are not at all hard to control, rather easy and amusing. It’s the damn AI that makes all the races so tryhard. You are in lead for 97% of the race and suddenly an AI got a God’s hand and achieved supersonic speed. If you are thinking of bumping into them and play dirty, well have fun bumping a rubber band. All these aspects are blades of the same sword. AI feels difficult- what a tryhard game/Thank God it’s not cheap easy. Perspective matters here. I am not against it. Surely it’s sometimes annoying, but it iz what it iz. 

It’s easy to understand how ground vehicles operate, steer, brake, drift, boost. But you are not familiar with aeroplane controls. Despite that, the first intro race makes you race an aeroplane. Instead of crossing checkpoints with my plane, I was crashing into enormous buildings and respawning. A terrible scenario that gets fixed in later event races where they teach you all aeroplane controls bit by bit.

[b]Open World-[/b]
Take on the American motorsports scene as you explore across the entire USA. Being able to drive different vehicles like cars, bikes, boats and planes in the same open-world means not only you are free to drift your car on street roads, tread speedboat through the waterways but fly high across the sky too. Befitting pillars for the open-world statement. Now we know there are no restrictions, but what about interactables? Unfortunately, that’s a guessing game. Oh, I have a sharp turn incoming and I have to drift? Let’s do this then. You are halfway in your drift airmailing all those bus shelters, mailboxes, lampposts in space, but suddenly you see a bench in between. That’s your stoppage. These randomly placed objects like benches or parked cars don’t follow Newton’s Law. They just wanna remain stationary no matter how hard you hit them. Trust me, these little objects ruined a lot of my lap times.

[b]Variety-[/b]
You can use the astonishing top-notch live map, which single-handedly increases the game score by 2. Like how they even made it render the entire game in a 3D model just by a single click. Moving forward, the complete map contains various types of events/races you can take part in. Just for clarification, there are not AI vs races only. You can take part in a race against time, drifting, freestyling and a lot of car chases too. As I said, you are buying a complete package of the racing genre with multiple vehicle types. But there seems to be a hollow part of the story. During cinematics, you can easily see the top-quality work put together and the exciting race descriptions they narrate. But in reality, you won’t find those races in action. One cinematic had an image of a monster truck jumping out of a plane with a parachute, but there’s nothing present like that. They escalated the expectations through cinematic dialogues but disappointed us in the end. It’s not completely devastating as the default variety is already more than enough.

[b]PvP/Grinding-[/b]
Sadly, you can’t run away from the “Look, there’s a level 1 guy with lvl99 car” scenario. It’s Ubisoft, which means expect a lot of transactions. Buy bundles, buy a season pass (Motorpass), or add in-game currency and get any high-speed car you want, but if you don’t wanna spend a penny, good luck grinding your a*s out. Be a part of a crew and evade the boredom of grinding alone.

[h1][b]📷Graphics:[/b][/h1]
Enjoy a pizza full of delicious and uplifting toppings added on a half-cooked bread base. Now all your bites will have a random taste. Some will please your tastebuds, and some will taste like cardboard. The object detailing in the open world is great, but their textures, Oh Lord. Never expected to witness those low texture brick buildings from a 2018 game. Like, come on; all the vehicles, roadside objects, even dirt tracks look so good. Then why the buildings and gravel roads look like a dusty mirror. To avoid these bad graphic races, I played air and water races the most.

[h1][b]📝Main Pros and Cons:[/b][/h1]

[b]Pros-[/b]
[list]
    [*]Big Open-world.
    [*]Character and vehicle customization.
    [*]Good chunk of playable time. 
    [*]Multiple vehicle types.
    [*]Varied races and challenges.
    [*]Offline or Online races.
[/list]

[b]Cons-[/b]
[list]
    [*]Grind vs PayToWin is real.
    [*]Semi cooked graphics.
    [*]Annoying indestructible objects.
    [*]No dynamic weather in the open world.
[/list]

[h1][b]🏷️Tips to new players:[/b][/h1]
Keep in mind, you can drift your plane. Without this, you are going to kiss the land whenever you take a flight. Don’t start PvP races until you reach at least the Famous rank. There are no restrictions on which racetrack to follow. So cut the track however you want. The first one to cross the checkpoint is the winner. Change resolution to borderless. Otherwise, whenever you will Alt+Tab, the game will start re-syncing, which wastes 4-10 seconds of your life every time.

[h1][b]😇Honest Rating:[/b][/h1]
If you are looking for that NFS arcade or real sim racing like Assetto Corsa and Project Cars, then just buy them instead. It’s nowhere perfect or overly marvellous. But I can assure you, if you invest enough hours into the game, you will adore it even as toxic relation. Only buy on big sale!

[h1] Stop Destroying Videogames [/h1]

[b]  European Citizens' Initiative :

Video games have grown into an industry with billions of customers worth hundreds of billions of euros. During this time, a specific business practice in the industry has been slowly emerging that is not only an assault on basic consumer rights but is destroying the medium itself.

An increasing number of publishers are selling video games that are required to connect through the internet to the game publisher, or "phone home" to function. While this is not a problem in itself, when support ends for these types of games, very often publishers simply sever the connection necessary for the game to function, proceed to destroy all working copies of the game, and implement extensive measures to prevent the customer from repairing the game in any way.

This practice is effectively robbing customers of their purchases and makes restoration impossible. Besides being an affront on consumer rights, video games themselves are unique creative works. Like film, or music, one cannot be simply substituted with another. By destroying them, it represents a creative loss for everyone involved and erases history in ways not possible in other mediums.

Existing laws and consumer agencies are ill-prepared to protect customers against this practice. The ability for a company to destroy an item it has already sold to the customer long after the fact is not something that normally occurs in other industries. With license agreements required to simply run the game, many existing consumer protections are circumvented. This practice challenges the concept of ownership itself, where the customer is left with nothing after "buying" a game.   

We wish to invoke Article 17 §1 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union [EUR-Lex - 12012P/TXT - EN - EUR-Lex (europa.eu)] – “No one may be deprived of his or her possessions, except in the public interest and in the cases and under the conditions provided for by law, subject to fair compensation being paid in good time for their loss.” – This practice deprives European citizens of their property by making it so that they lose access to their product an indeterminate/arbitrary amount of time after the point of sale. We wish to see this remedied, at the core of this Initiative. 

We also invoke Title XV of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU)[EUR-Lex - 12012E/TXT - EN - EUR-Lex (europa.eu)] and the following TFEU Articles as our justification for and the Union’s imperative to respond to this initiative:

Article 169 – Per §1, the EU has an obligation “to promote the interests of consumers and to ensure a high level of consumer protection…to protecting the health, safety and economic interests of consumers”. We believe this practice infringes upon or requires correction to be commensurate with the EU’s obligation. The actions taken in response to this initiative must supersede any end user license agreements associated with videogames.  

Article 12 – “Consumer protection requirements shall be taken into account in defining and implementing other Union policies and activities.” Given that this practice extends across Member States and beyond the EU, the Union’s actions regarding this practice ought to keep consumer protection in mind. The actions taken in response to this initiative must supersede any end user license agreements associated with video games.

Article 114, §3 – “The Commission, in its proposals envisaged in paragraph 1 concerning health, safety, environmental protection and consumer protection, will take as a base a high level of protection… Within their respective powers, the European Parliament and the Council will also seek to achieve this objective” This practice undermines the high level of consumer protection that the Commission, the European Parliament, and the Council takes as the basis of law in the Union, and their objectives of establishing and maintaining the functioning of an internal market as described in §1 of this Article, and Article 26 TFEU.[/b]

OK.  I'm going to write this as someone who has been a huge fan of The Crew franchise.  The short answer is, "Yes.  I'd recommend this game."  The longer answer is a little more nuanced and if you'd like to read a few "caveats" from someone who still enjoys the game, mostly......please proceed.

I have played this game since launch.  I owned the "Gold Edition" on PS4 and logged A LOT of hours there.  I then made the switch to PC and, as you can see, I've logged over 200 more hours on here.  There are a lot of positives that any number of other reviews will also bring up.  There are also a lot of negatives, many of which are not immediately apparent.  And here is where I am going to bring these up.  They weren't severe enough for me to not recommend the game, but they were important enough for me to mention.

1.  No cross-platform support or cross-play (not too concerned about cross-play though)

It's one thing to not offer this.  It's another to have very specific rewards for completing certain events and not allow people who earned those rewards to carry them over (or even allow them to use MTX to buy them back on your new platform).  Don't get me wrong, if they asked me to pay money for items I already earned; I'd tell them to get bent.  However, this business model here actively discourages people from buying the game on more than one platform.  Seems stupid.  I have numerous cars earned from PS4 Summit, but because my Uplay account is logged in to a steam version of the game instead of a PS4 version of the game......I can't use them.

2.  It's pitched as "any vehicle, anywhere, any time"

No.  It's not.  Sure, there are plenty of events and lots of different vehicles, but the lion's share of events and vehicles fall in to "street race".  There are more "street race" events than all the other "Street HQ" events combined.  There are more hypercars and street race cars than any other class except for MAYBE Rally Raid and Touring Car.  I don't mind these events/vehicles, but it would be nice to get something else.  It's especially bad for Summit as most "special vehicle rewards" are just another street spec or hypercar spec.  The "Xtreme Series" (one of the more unique aspects of the game) has less than ten events and that's after they added some.

3.  It's "grindy".

Again, clearly I don't mind the grind, but I'd be lying if I said a large majority of my time spent wasn't re-running the same handful of events for cash and parts.  The RNG is hell sometimes and certain vehicle types just get aggravating to get parts for.  

For example.  I own full legendary part sets on every single hypercar I own.  I managed to do this in about a week simply re-running the New York hypercar event,  It nets about 300,000 bucks on Ace and yields a BUNCH of legendary parts.  The event is a long cross-country event and takes around 30 min to complete.  Simple enough.  Jump on, run it once or twice, net cash and parts.  But outside hypercars (and one or two street race events) there aren't any events like this for the other specs.  This is ESPECIALLY egregious, because they had stuff like that in the first Crew.  It would be nice if there was a better way of earning legendary sets without relying on Summit or getting to Icon 1000+ to dump a bunch of points in to buffing your loot quality and amount.  

4.  "Vanity Parts" and "Premium Currency"

I have an issue with "pay to customize", especially on a game where customizing is a key component to that experience.  It's one thing to pay $5 to have a gold gimp suit or some such crap on Battlefield or CoD.  It's another to have these "pay parts" on a game all about customizing.  It's made worse by the "Season Passes" having a "regular" and a "premium" version and even the premium pass doesn't net you enough Crew Credits to buy an epic vanity part.  You get a couple extra vehicles (probably another street spec or hypercar).

I mostly bring this up because they used to gift Crew Credits a bunch more and just by saving up a bit, you could put them to use in amazing ways and made you WANT to play.

5.  The "Online" Experience.

It's not great.  It's better than a lot I've seen, but it's still pretty bad.  I've had invites from all kinds of people,  almost none that actually want to do events.  You join someone's crew, you screw around on the map until someone gets bored.  Someone joins YOUR crew, they quit as soon as they realize you're starting an event.  Maybe it's time.  Maybe it's the platform.  I can't say for sure.  I CAN say, the social experience WAS better when I was on PS4.

Last but not least, this isn't Forza.  If you're expecting Forza, then buy Forza.  This is more akin to the GOOD Need for Speeds from back in the day (i.e. Most Wanted, Carbon, Underground).  The physics aren't great, but they aren't horrible.  It's mostly just designed to goof off with and have a good time......not recreating what driving a Bugatti is like.

If nothing I said dissuaded you, then give it a try.....and if you see me around, shoot me an invite.  Just don't be afraid of doing something.

After 50 hours, The Crew 2 has left me with a lot of wonderful memories. They aren't filled with the kind of emergent stories you get from exploring an open world and its systems, nor are they moments that involve goofing around with strangers--The Crew 2 is lacking in both those aspects. Instead, my memories are filled with the game's variety of vehicular activities and the wonderfully curated tracks: the unrealistic, the impossible, and the delightful.

It's surprising to see just how much The Crew 2 differs from the original game. There's been a noticeable shift in Ubisoft’s last few open-world titles, one that's moving toward a focus on player-driven progression--large selections of optional activities, non-linear structures, rewards for doing just about anything--and The Crew 2 benefits significantly from this direction. The gritty crime angle from the original game is gone, and instead, The Crew 2 takes reams of pages from the book of Forza Horizon. The game centers on a nationwide festival of motorsports where you, a rookie, are poised to become the next big star. While the setup is conventional, and the focus on social media fame is obnoxious, what it brings to the game is a colorful and upbeat vibe, an impressive variety of different disciplines, and positively ridiculous arcade driving on land, water, and through the air.

Despite the game's focus on real-world branding and mimicry of televised motorsports, The Crew 2's greatest asset is its willingness to be ridiculous. Races in The Crew 2 might involve jumping your street-racing car off skyscrapers, or your powerboat off the Hoover Dam. They might include making high-speed touring cars go head to head through the tight, windy Hollywood Hills, and motocross bikes take jumps across shipping freighters and freeways right before you transform into a prop plane like some kind of extreme-sports mecha. This is a game that will cover Los Angeles in three feet of snow for no logical reason other than icy roads make for more thrilling street races. Abundant nitro boosts, uncomplicated drifting, and generous rubber-banding also help keep the act of driving exciting when things are relatively tame.

As a game with an open world, races and challenges can naturally be found and initiated when you stumble across them at particular points on the map. However, playing The Crew 2 with open-world exploration as your primary means of moving from activity to activity reveals the game's major downfall: it's too big, and all the activities and interesting locations are too spread out. The game hides a number of boxes with vehicle components across the map, which you can hunt for using a proximity tracker, but even these feel too few and far between.

But with that in mind, The Crew 2 thankfully makes it easy to cut your commute down via player-friendly shortcuts. The game has an option to view all 120+ primary activities and countless more skill challenges (featuring things like escapes, slaloms, and a rewarding photo mode) in a categorized, list-style view, with the option to not just set a waypoint to them, but instantly start them no matter where you are in the world, at no cost. The loading times in The Crew 2 are impressively brief all around, so if you want to, you can churn through races and challenges back-to-back to very quickly and efficiently rack up progression points, earn cash, and set leaderboard positions from the moment you start.

It's an option that's both convenient and gives the impression that the game is conscious of your time. Likewise, any activity can be restarted or aborted in seconds if you're having a bad run, and there's a quick back-on-track feature that can be used any time. When you're not in an event you can switch to any vehicle you own immediately, without penalty, and without having to go anywhere. That's on top of being able to assign a favorite ground vehicle, boat, and plane to your right analog stick to allow for instantaneous switching during free-roam exploration, which provides its own kind of fun, for example, flying into the stratosphere with your plane before switching to a boat and careening back to Earth. Any vehicle that's available for sale is also graciously available for you to test drive on a moment's notice.

The variety of different vehicular disciplines in The Crew 2 is downright impressive--each of the 14 styles is tangibly unique from one another. Every time I started to get fatigued with one method of competition, I could quickly jump to another that had a completely different feel. Each is housed within one of four "Families" which you're free to move between to perpetuate your overall progress: Street (street racing, drifting, drag racing, long-distance hypercar racing), Offroad (cross-country rally raid, motocross, loose-surface rallycross), Freestyle (plane aerobatics, jet sprint boating, monster trucking), and Pro (power boating, air racing, touring cars, and grand prix).

While the execution of The Crew 2's disciplines might not wholly satisfy purists of any one given style, it does a great job of making each feel accessible, fun, and unique. I'm usually too intimidated by grand prix racing to give it a shot in other games, and I would never have even considered the idea of playing a power boating game. But, the Crew 2 encourages you to try a little bit of everything, and it's easy thanks to the game's approachable arcade-style mechanics, as well as the prospects of seeing more beautiful and ludicrous tracks.

And whether you're driving, boating, or flying across The Crew 2's America, it's a mostly beautiful journey. The game's natural environments, particularly bodies of water and the sky, look fantastic, as do weather effects like snow and rain. All are enhanced to breathtaking heights by the superb lighting, though the continuous day/night and weather cycle can be an occasional inconvenience during some events--whether it be afternoon sun in your eyes, snow obscuring track obstacles, or having to fly through a tight canyon in complete darkness. Where the visuals visibly falter are in dense urban areas. You likely won't notice buildings when you're zooming past them at 200km/h, but any slower and you can't help but notice how plain they are, especially in broad daylight with clear skies. Character models, on the other hand, always look incredibly basic, no matter the situation.

The game's RPG-style vehicle upgrade system returns from the original game, though it still doesn't feel particularly meaningful. You'll receive loot after every race in various stages of rarity (common, uncommon, rare, epic), and each corresponds to a particular vehicle part and has its own power number, which contributes to your vehicle's overall power number. There is some small benefit to this system--all vehicles of a particular class, despite having different power levels in their stock configuration, will max out at the same number, meaning you can stick with your favorite car all the way up to and through the endgame.

I'm annoyed by the game's lack of public interaction and meaningless gear system, but I'll fondly recall both the tension of flinging sprint boats back and forth through the narrow, artificial canals of The Venetian in Las Vegas, and the easygoing satisfaction of an hour-long hypercar race from New York to San Francisco, where I listened to a podcast and enjoyed the rolling scenery. Despite its shortcomings, The Crew 2 still displays admirable strengths, which lie in its player-friendly features, freedom of movement, and its willingness to bend the rules in order to make things exciting and varied for an accessible, American-themed thrillride.

          -The Crew 2 is not easy to complete, but it is easy to manage and observe the progress. Each discipline comes with a percentage of completion. In game, there is also an option to pin desired missions to track progress real time.

You can just do it.

Yeah go on.

5/10 - Lots to like, but lots to hate. Could have been so much more. Full review below:

= Intro =

Sometimes, I'm in the mood for a racer. I fondly remember the days of NFSU 2, Gran Turismo on the PS and Most Wanted, games that not only lasted me weeks, but gave me new bands to listen to and endless replay value. Had this on my 'to play' list so got around to it. Enjoyed Forza, but it felt a bit flat and I wanted something with a bit more progression.

= Gameplay =

This is a racing game. Vrooom, cars go fast. But it's also a watersports game. And an offroad game. And a rally game. And a flying stunts game. And a flying racer game. And another dozen types of racing/stunt game rolled into one. Oh and also a loot game. You can see the problem immediately.

That said, man - this game does try. And sometimes gets it right. The water racing is immensely fun. Rally racing is great. Motorcross is mostly a blast. The absolute apex of the game for me are the lengthy 'runs' - massive races between cities, that lead you through towns, cities, mountains, forests etc. Glorious.

The weakest part of the game for me has to be the street racing, which isn't the nice, varied, speedy tracks you are likely expecting, but rather boxy, twisty monstrosities filled with right-angle turns. Right off the bat, these were frustrating as heck and some of the later ones will make you want to eat a kitten.

This has to do with the fact that a lot of cars handle like shopping carts and the more expensive ones handle like shopping carts with a jet booster. This game works best with long, open tracks, which sadly are lacking in a lot of styles.

Beyond this, every 'discipline' has it's own set of vehicles and loot. Welcome to the grind overdrive. And this is made worse by the fact that the sheer number of event types means that many only get a handful of races, total.

However the kicker is the AI. It...cheats. Rubberbanding is utterly crazy, especially when you start doing higher difficulty races - but unlike other games, it's only applied to give the AI an advantage. If you fail to drive perfectly on some tracks, the AI will soar past you instantly. Or it may just randomly do that anyway.

However once the AI is ahead, it just keeps on going. This is especially evident in the set-vehicle races where you and the AI have (allegedly) the same vehicles and specs. However, on Ace, you can enjoy the sight of the AI flying into the distance right from the get go, waving and flipping the bird.

This leads to a lot of styles being not only about driving prowess but luck, and finding ways to break the game. Weird, unmarked shortcuts, odd physics and the like. Sigh.

All of that said though, I don't hate this game. When it works, it works like gangbusters. Maybe if they had removed the boring flying stuff and produced double the races for existing styles, this could have been a winner.

= Graphics and Audio =

Visually, this game is a mixed bag. Water is lovely. Weather is beautiful. Lighting can be stunning. But textures are meh and ...wow, do cities look awful. Especially at daytime. Framerates are perfect.

Audio, rather than the mix of metal, rock, punk, rap and EDM you may be expecting is instead a small collection of the blandest EDM known to man. 

= Style =

As I've said - too cluttered, too thinly spread.

And the interface/design is a nightmare. Let's say you do a race a few times, restarting immediately after you finish. Your loot goes to the mailbox. You then need to leave the race (loading time), go to a racing base (loading time), walk around, get the mail, exit the base (loading time), go to your home (loading time), walk up to your vehicle stand, change your vehicle (loading time) and then upgrade it.

Welcome to busywork.

But the absolute worst thing for me was discovering, after returning to the game after a long period, that there was no way to reset progress, whatsoever. Meaning if you experiment early and foul things up, there is no way to ever remedy it.

= Value =

To be fair, there is a lot here for the price, especially if you get this game on it's frequent, really good specials.

There are microtransactions, but most of the stuff can be earned in-game. However there is also stuff that can't. And I'm sick of microtransactions in AAA priced games.

= Overall =

+ Many events are insanely fun
+ Original and well implemented loot system
+ 'Run' races are just awesome

- Impossible to ever reset progress/start a new game
- Insanely cheaty AI
- Frustrating street racing
- Awful interface
- Open world feels meaningless
- Spread way too thin
- Ubisoft style microtransactions

At the end of the day, this is a game I really want to like. With a bit more focus, less insane design decisions and some better/more interesting tracks, this could have been amazing. As it is...it's both enjoyable enough to keep me playing and flawed enough to make this hard to recommend.

This game has received a lot of hate. Personally, I believe a lot of the hate it undeserved, but they can make some good points.

Starting with the pros:
- Vehicle variety and detail. This game has over 300 different vehicles, and personally I believe the detail on the vehicles is out standing, even things as small as bolts for some extended fenders:   10/10

- Vehicle Customisation. Almost all of the vehicles have a wide range of changeable parts. There are many options to choose from in an easy to navigate menu, as well as bonus items that can be rewarded from playing the game by doing daily missions giving you a currency to buy special items such as under glow, custom wheels, tire smoke and more.         9/10

- The Map Size. The map size is where this game stands out above all. In a fast car (280Mph top speed+) with good driving it took me over an hour to travel from the southeast tip to the north west tip. In this map you will find several cities and other land marks along the way, also encountering the occasional player along your journey. The details in the cities are spectacular and the amount of places to go are countless.     10/10

- Multiplayer. The game puts you into a public lobby filled with usually around 3 to 8 other players, communicating with a custom chat menu which prevents and toxicity or bullying. When you want to play alone you can but on the other hand if you are looking to go on a road trip with a friend or do some races with a pal this game has made an easy system for you to do so.       8/10

- Race Variety. Currently in the game there and 16 different Motorsports events to choose from:
      -Street Race, Drift, Drag race, Hyper car
      -Motor cross, Hovercraft, Rally cross ( off-road ), Rally raid
      -Freestyle ( Stunt planes), jet sprint ( Small boat racing ), demo derby, Monster truck
      -Touring car, F1, Boat racing, Air race
Along with these you get different skill based activities like Speed-traps and escapes ( furthest distance in a period of time ) as well as Photo ops of landmarks or player scenarios.          10/10

- The Summit. Every week, there is a series of events that you can do competing against other players in order to win prices such as followers, parts or occasionally, cars. This feature gives a deep purpose to this game, and for me a feeling like i need and want to come back to do those races and get those prizes. 10/10

Smaller mentions:
-Unlimited garage space
-Customisable car settings and parts
-As you level up, you will receive rewards at certain milestones ( Cars planes boats etc )


And now the Cons:

-Graphics. This game can look beautiful, however a lot of the places feel empty or dull, like they need something extra. Also, the shading was poorly made, with a lot of colours looking flat. Like I said, certain places look fantastic and are very photogenic, however the textures aren't HD and could have more colour. With a simple graphics remake this game could easily be level with GTA V or FH4.     3.5/10

-Sound. Some of the car sounds are well executed, but for the most part they seem dull and like they could be more intense. The vehicles that do sound good are incredible, however a lot of cars that seem powerful get underwhelmed by the sounds coming from the engine.  4/10

-Weather. Now when i say weather I need to make it VERY clear i mean the weather changing, not the visuals. In my opinion, the rain in this game falls just short of GTA V rain puddles in the city at night, but with this game you can be in sunny weather, you go into settings to maybe turn your sound down a little and when you are out of the menu, boom: Thick snow. Even when it changes visibly to the player, it is too fast and too frequent. 5/10

-The Voices. Oh my lord turn off voices and turn on subtitles because the majority of the voices in this game are infuriating and get super annoying super quick.     1.5/10

-The prices. The vehicle prices can be realistic and occasionally generous, with a Buggati Chiron costing 2.4 million, but then when you venture over to the low end of the spectrum like bikes, you start to see prices like 500 grand for a sports bike. It isn't accurate. Another thing to mention is the grind for money. The money received after a race needs to increase, as grinding mindlessly for 3 hours in order to save up 2.4 million like I have done gets quite frustrating, and whilst it normally pays off, the pain you feel inside when you know the only way to get yourself that money you need for your next car is going to take 100 races of the same race is discomforting and off-putting.

Important note: i see a lot of people talking about rubber banding and i need to say i have never experienced this. I often finish races 10-30 seconds ahead when i use my super fast vehicles, and on other races like the 40 minute race it is often minutes ahead. If there was rubber banding, how could the times they are behind me be so large?

To summarise, I am saying this game is worth it, but keep it in your wishlist until it is on a sale to make up for the cons you may experience in this game.

There's also a good, active community that keeps adding custom liveries (skins/vinyls) which you can apply to your cars directly. And of course, there's a decent liverly editor too.

4. Race tracks: Challenging and fun race tracks. Some even have good shortcuts which you can master by driving repeatedly. You may try to break some of the world records.

5. Diversity: Various disciplines to choose from. You ever get bored from the street races, you can do boat race, jet race, air race, motorbike race, monster trucks, you name it. Although the game has good diversity, it's biased towards street races due to the number of events available in it compared to other disciplines. But then, if you're a street racing fan, that's what you want.

6. Regular content update: Really impressed with the 'Live Summit' weekly events with unique themes. You compete with other players to get the prizes. Prizes being special edition cars, tires, car parts, nitros, followers, etc.

CONS:

1. Graphics: Being a 2018 game, the graphics could've been better. You can't expect amazing graphics for such a giant map but the textures and reflections could still be better (as they're reused a lot). The lightings/weather system is good during the day with bright sunlight but it looks like a water painting when cloudy or rainy. The nights are okay at best.

2. Unbalanced AI: The AI in the game is somewhat unbalanced. I mean you can easily win street races or hypercars in Ace (highest difficulty) with a decent, well-upgraded car. Like a Buggati Divo or La Voiture Noire. But then you'll sweat to finish even the 'Easy' drag races without grinding.

3. Physics: Funny. If you're looking for a racing game with realistic or good physics, this isn't the one. They've surely made the car handling better with each update, but it still hurts to see a hypercar wobble at 400+ kmph with slight curves.

4. Optimization: I'm not sure how it scored 7/10 on GameDebate for optimization. I have a good GPU. Though it runs smooth most of the time, a crowded street race or a multiplayer with varied ping rates would cause immediate lags. Sometimes even kick players out. Even the processor and the GPU runs hotter during the gameplay as compared to other games of the same scale.

5. PvP: There's no customizability for PvP races. Also, the PvP player base is low and often results in a long waiting time.

If you're a racing freak who loves arcade and don't mind a bit of a funny physics, go get it. You won't regret. If you're into simulators and graphics, stay away. I've been a Forza fan myself (have a good amount of hours spent on the windows store version), but this game is still very fun in what it offers.

The Crew 2 has got the potential for a good arcade racing game. Unfortunately it's not. 

While the graphics look nice and the cars offer very good feedback, the whole setting sucks. The story makes you want to turn of your PC as soon as those ai smart asses, you have to team up with, start talking. Their constant advice makes you want to throw up, run away or punch them in the face. And they keep talking all the time.

Of course you're a rookie driving your way up to stardom by collecting followers. The dream of every six year old.

And of course your path to the top is riddled with obstacles. At least that's something Ubisoft really does well. Especially when this concept forces players to pay real money to overcome the hindrances.

Your main hindrance are cars because you ain't got none. Or should I say almost none. The standard version of The Crew 2 gives you a slow street car, a slow plane and a slow boat. At least this allows you to play some races. 

You need to win races to gain followers. Ending games in first, second or third position also grants you upgrades for your vehicle.

Additionally you earn in-game money. In-game money is needed to buy new cars, planes or boats. And that's exactly where Ubisofts sales department steps in. In order to shorten the tedious task of endlessly driving races to win the money necessary to buy cars for different events or higher racing classes, you can simply buy in-game money with real money. 

You can also buy the season pass which grants you two new cars every month for one year and an in-game discount when buying new cars. Of course the season pass costs real money.

You also need the best cars in order to compete with other players in multi-player mode. It will take you a lot of racing time winning the necessary in-game money to buy the cars needed to beat the competition. And you also need to upgrade the cars.

No matter what type of car you buy, you always receive the standard edition. So you need to drive races with this car to add upgrades. 

There's a lot of work to get the cars you need. And Ubisoft made sure that there are many different vehicles you need.

- Street Race
- Drift
- Drag Race
- Hyper Car
- Rally Raid
- Moto Cross
- Rally Cross
- Aerobatics
- Jetsprint
- Monster Truck
- Powerboat
- Touring Car
- Air Race

In order to stand a chance in multi-player mode you need to learn the tracks including all shortcuts. Thankfully the multi-player tracks are the same as the single-player races. This gives you the chance to train and memorize routes.

Contrary to The Crew 1 the USA is no longer the star of the game. Although graphics have improved, villages and cities look exchangeable. The unique atmosphere of Chicago, New York, San Francisco or Miami is no longer perceptible in The Crew 2. Even the countryside sometimes looks artificial. Not everywhere, but in some places. 

At some locations it seems as if the developers didn't finish designing the landscape. There are areas where bushes and trees seem to be missing and hills are bald.

Free riding is no longer fun. That's because other cars drive closer together. The Crew 1 allowed you to race top speed in the middle of the highway passing cars on both sides. Try that in The Crew 2 and you will constantly crash.

You often find places where the game tells you to take a photo. You'll get an achievement once you took 40 photos in unique places. If you tell the game to mark the spot for the photo nothing is marked. You'll start searching but don't know where to go. There's no mark at all and neither navigation not mini-map can guide you. Then you take a photo and still have 40 photos left to take.

The same applies for extra upgrades. Extra upgrades are scattered all over the US. Once you move close to an upgrade your navigation system starts blinking and pinging. But if you search for the upgrade it's nowhere to be found. At least I can't find them. In 20 hours play time I found a single upgrade. It was a huge shining blue box on a field, twice as big as my car and it could not be missed. But whenever I search for them in a city they are nowhere to be found. Not sure if it's me but it's frustrating. I think it's bugged or again unfinished development.

I'd say this game is worth a try. There’s plenty of racing, though it’s kind of like the towers in Assassin’s Creed or Far Cry—you’re constantly grinding for something.

About that grind: collecting tuning parts (to get bonuses, you need to put together a full set of the same color and type) can be a hassle. Don’t expect to complete a set easily—you’ll likely be replaying the same race multiple times. There are around 200 races in total, each with three difficulty levels. I’ve cleared 88% of the main races and about 51% of the three other categories, and I’m nowhere near completing a full set on any car. But honestly, you don't need a full set. Once you max out your car’s power, you can just blow past the AI ​​opponents and enjoy the view.

And the views here are worth it. The game is gorgeous, and the scale is impressive. You truly feel like you’re driving across an entire country. The map might even be bigger than Euro Truck Simulator's, even with all the DLC. Each state has its own distinct look and vibe, and I loved the variety.

The one downside is that the game kind of forces you to try different modes. I wasn’t really into planes or Off-Road, though the boat races were surprisingly fun. Some modes just feel pointless, like Derby. It’s just cars bouncing around with no real destruction physics. And F1 racing doesn’t really fit either—the arcade physics don’t do it justice, and when you’re driving an F1 car off-road, it’s just weird.

At first, I hated Off-Road races and was ready to skip them. I tried MX, Aerobatics, and Touring Car instead, but that sense of “incomplete” pushed me to finish those 20 Off-Road races, unlock the boss, and complete all the achievements.

Overall, the game’s pretty easy—maybe too easy. To make it more challenging, you’d have to clear everything on the easiest difficulty first, and with a game this big, that can get tiring. I put in 30 hours and only got through half the game. I really enjoyed the hypercars, though; I’d be down for even more long races that last an hour or more. There’s something special about speeding down a wide-open highway, listening to music, and soaking up the graphics.

In short, there’s something for everyone here, so I’d say it’s worth a thumbs-up.

The Crew 2 is not a bad game; you just need to understand what it is. It’s an arcade racer probably the most arcade one you can find. I’d even say that some Need for Speed titles feel more realistic than this.

I was mainly comparing it to Forza Horizon 4. I decided to install both at the same time and play a bit of TC2 and FH4. In the end, Forza 4 appealed to me much more. It doesn’t have planes or boats, which for me is actually a plus - I play these games to drive cars.

Another important detail is vehicle handling. Because The Crew 2 has a larger, more diverse map and a wider variety of vehicles  motorcycles, cars, boats, and planes - the physics for all of them feels simplified, I’d even say primitive. When you switch from an SUV to a regular sedan, you barely feel any difference, even though you should.

In FH4, when I drive the same car and switch from tarmac to dirt, I can feel the difference immediately, and I actually need to go into tuning settings to adapt the car to the type of race.

In The Crew 2, it really doesn’t matter. You just hold the throttle and spam nitro. A few more downsides besides physics are the sounds and the first-person view  both are poorly made. It’s clear the game was designed around the third-person camera, focusing on the “fun arcade” vibe.

Yes, the big map of the USA is nice, and it’s cool to visit different cities, but everything feels toy-like.

The only real positives are the large map and the wide selection of vehicles, but even those lead to many of the downsides I already mentioned. So my rating is 5/10. Still, for fans of pure arcade games, it should be enjoyable. Whether we like it or not, Forza Horizon 4 is also an arcade racer, but it has more simulation-like elements, so I prefer it.
